analysis.one_liner: Replaces all private health insurance with a single government plan covering every resident at no out-of-pocket cost.
analysis.headline: Despite 124 House cosponsors, the bill sat in three committees for two years without a single markup or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a government-run health program covering every U.S. resident, with no deductibles, copayments, or coinsurance. It would cover doctor visits, hospital care, prescription drugs, dental, vision, hearing, mental health, and long-term care. Private insurers would be barred from selling coverage that duplicates the program's benefits, and for-profit hospitals that want to participate would have to convert to nonprofit status. The program would be funded by redirecting existing federal health spending and new taxes on top earners, payroll, unearned income, and stock and bond trades. The bill was referred to three House committees and never received a hearing, markup, or vote in either chamber.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. resident, who would receive comprehensive coverage with no premiums, deductibles, or copays; the roughly one in ten Americans without insurance would gain coverage, and people with high out-of-pocket costs or coverage gaps would see them disappear. Hospitals and clinics would also be freed from billing insurers, and low-income households would no longer pay for care they previously could not afford.
analysis.who_benefits_short: All U.S. residents, especially the uninsured

how_it_helps.text: All individuals residing in the United States and its territories would be covered, receiving a program card by mail and presumed eligible when they present for care [S3].

Coverage includes all medically necessary care with no deductibles, copayments, coinsurance, or other cost-sharing, spanning primary and hospital care, prescription drugs, long-term care, mental health, full dental, vision, and hearing services including hearing aids [S3].
Patients keep free choice of participating doctors and hospitals, and benefits are portable through any licensed clinician anywhere in the country [S3].
Prescription drug prices would be negotiated annually by the program, with bulk procurement and a formulary that promotes generic use [S3].
Clerical, billing, and administrative workers whose jobs are eliminated would get first priority in retraining and two years of salary-parity transition benefits capped at $100,000 per year [S3].

analysis.who_pays: New taxes fall on the top 5% of income earners, on payroll and self-employment income through a progressive excise tax, on unearned income, and on stock and bond transactions. Private health insurers lose their core market, and investor-owned hospitals and clinics that want to participate must convert to nonprofit status, compensated for reasonable losses over 15 years through Treasury bonds.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners and the insurance industry

drawbacks.text: The program is funded by five new or redirected revenue streams, including higher personal income taxes on the top 5% of earners, a progressive payroll and self-employment excise tax, a tax on unearned income, and a tax on stock and bond transactions [S3] — a large tax increase whose full annual cost is not estimated anywhere in the bill.

Private insurers would be barred from selling coverage that duplicates the program's benefits, meaning Americans who prefer private plans could no longer buy one for covered services [S3]; this is the strongest objection from those who value choice of private insurance.

Institutions may participate only if they are public or nonprofit; for-profit hospitals and clinics must convert to nonprofit status with owner compensation for reasonable financial losses over 15 years [S3], a sweeping restructuring of the provider industry.

Provider payment would run through annually negotiated global budgets and fee schedules under a government director rather than market rates [S3]; the long-standing criticism of such systems is that underfunded budgets can produce payment cuts, strained capacity, or waits for care.

Hundreds of thousands of insurance and billing jobs would be eliminated by design; the bill addresses this with two years of transition pay and retraining priority, but the disruption to those workers and their communities is real [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to ordinary people are large and direct: universal coverage with no out-of-pocket costs, including services most current plans skip, like dental, hearing, and long-term care. The costs are also large and concentrated: substantially higher taxes on high earners and investment income, the elimination of the private insurance market for covered care, and a mandatory conversion of for-profit providers. Independent cost estimates were never done for this version, so whether new taxes would fully cover the expanded benefits is untested. It is an ambitious restructuring whose design leaves major questions — total cost, transition disruption, and rationing under global budgets — to be resolved in implementation.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees and its subcommittees in early 2017, and in two years none of them ever reported it out, so it never reached a vote on the House floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers Jr. (D-MI) introduced the bill on January 24, 2017, with 50 original cosponsors [S1] [S5].
The same day, the Speaker referred it to three committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Natural Resources — each for consideration only of provisions in its own jurisdiction [S5].
Within weeks it was further referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee and the Natural Resources Subcommittee on Indian, Insular and Alaska Native Affairs, where it stayed [S5].
Over the two-year Congress, no committee held a markup or reported the bill, and no vote ever occurred in the House [S1] [S5].
After Rep. Conyers resigned in December 2017, Rep. Keith Ellison (D-MN) was recognized as the new first sponsor for purposes of adding cosponsors, by unanimous consent in March 2018 [S5].
By the end of the Congress the bill had accumulated 124 cosponsors, all of them Democrats [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing health insurance industry and for-profit providers, whose market was preserved because the bill never advanced; ordinary Americans' coverage and out-of-pocket costs are unchanged.

sides.party_line_note: All 124 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; the bill was referred under a Republican majority and never advanced.

industries.note: Insurers would be barred from selling any coverage duplicating the program's benefits, which would end their core market for medical insurance; they could sell only coverage for non-medically-necessary services like cosmetic surgery. The bill's death preserved their existing business, which is funded by premiums and out-of-pocket costs borne by ordinary people.

No institution could participate in the program unless it was public or nonprofit; for-profit providers would have to convert, with owners compensated for reasonable financial losses over 15 years through Treasury bond sales. Their continued for-profit status under the status quo depends on revenue from patient payments and insurance reimbursement.

The program would negotiate drug prices annually, procure medications in bulk, and run a formulary favoring generics, ending the current system in which Medicare is legally barred from directly negotiating prices and patients pay list prices out of pocket. Drug makers keep that pricing power because the bill never advanced.

Reduced paperwork would eliminate many clerical, billing, and administrative jobs at insurers, doctors' offices, and hospitals — the bill anticipates this and offers first priority in retraining plus two years of salary-parity transition pay capped at $100,000 a year. These workers' interests run with the public's in wanting secure livelihoods, but the bill restructures their industry.
